```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(lab4)
library(caret)
library(mlbench)
```

## 1. The train/test split of the BostonHousing data

The data are split into a training set (80%) and a test set (20%) using
`caret::createDataPartition()`.

```{r split}
data("BostonHousing", package = "mlbench")
set.seed(2026)
idx   <- createDataPartition(BostonHousing$medv, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)
train <- BostonHousing[idx, ]
test  <- BostonHousing[-idx, ]
c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test))
```

All models use `medv` (median house value) as the response and 10-fold
cross-validation on the training set.

```{r ctrl}
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)
```

## 2. Linear regression and forward selection

First, an ordinary linear regression using all covariates, evaluated with
10-fold cross-validation on the training set.

```{r lm}
lm_fit <- train(medv ~ ., data = train, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
lm_fit
```

Forward selection is done with `leapForward`. By default caret tries only a
few values of `nvmax`, so the tuning grid is set to every size from 1 to 13
covariates. `BostonHousing` has 14 columns, one of which is the response
`medv`, so there are 13 predictors (`chas` becomes the dummy `chas1`).
Because `leapForward` cannot fit zero covariates, the intercept-only model is
fitted separately with `method = "null"`, so that all sizes from 0 to 13 are
compared.

```{r fwd}
fwd_fit <- train(medv ~ ., data = train, method = "leapForward",
                 tuneGrid = data.frame(nvmax = 1:13), trControl = ctrl)

null_fit <- train(medv ~ ., data = train, method = "null", trControl = ctrl)

fwd_tab <- rbind(
  data.frame(nvmax = 0, RMSE = null_fit$results$RMSE),
  fwd_fit$results[, c("nvmax", "RMSE")]
)
fwd_tab
fwd_fit$bestTune
summary(fwd_fit$finalModel)$outmat[fwd_fit$bestTune$nvmax, ]
```

The table shows that all model sizes from 0 to 13 were evaluated. Forward
selection chose `nvmax = X` covariates, with a cross-validated RMSE of Y,
compared with Z for the full linear regression.

## 3. Evaluating the performance on the training set

```{r train-perf}
train_perf <- rbind(
  lm      = postResample(predict(lm_fit,  train), train$medv),
  forward = postResample(predict(fwd_fit, train), train$medv)
)
train_perf
```

## 4. Ridge regression with `ridgereg()` as a custom caret model

```{r ridge-method}
ridge_method <- list(
  label = "ridgereg", library = "lab4", type = "Regression",
  parameters = data.frame(parameter = "lambda", class = "numeric",
                          label = "Lambda"),
  grid = function(x, y, len = NULL, search = "grid") {
    data.frame(lambda = 10^seq(-3, 3, length.out = len))
  },
  fit = function(x, y, wts, param, lev, last, weights, classProbs, ...) {
    dat <- as.data.frame(x)
    dat$.outcome <- y
    lab4::ridgereg(.outcome ~ ., data = dat, lambda = param$lambda)
  },
  predict = function(modelFit, newdata, preProc = NULL, submodels = NULL) {
    predict(modelFit, as.data.frame(newdata))
  },
  prob = NULL,
  sort = function(x) x[order(-x$lambda), ]
)
```

## 5. Choosing lambda with 10-fold cross-validation

The ridge model is trained for 30 values of lambda, log-spaced between 0.001
and 1000. For each value, 10-fold cross-validation on the training set gives
an estimate of RMSE, and the lambda with the lowest CV RMSE is selected.

```{r ridge-fit}
set.seed(2026)
ridge_fit <- train(medv ~ ., data = train, method = ridge_method,
                   trControl = ctrl,
                   tuneGrid = data.frame(lambda = 10^seq(-3, 3, length.out = 30)))
ridge_fit$bestTune
ridge_fit$results[, c("lambda", "RMSE", "Rsquared")]
plot(ridge_fit, scales = list(x = list(log = 10)))
```

## 6. Evaluation on the test set

```{r test-perf}
test_perf <- rbind(
  lm      = postResample(predict(lm_fit,    test), test$medv),
  forward = postResample(predict(fwd_fit,   test), test$medv),
  ridge   = postResample(predict(ridge_fit, test), test$medv)
)
round(test_perf, 3)
```

### Concluding comments

On the test set, ridge regression has the lowest RMSE (4.634), followed by forward selection (4.660) and the full linear model (4.665). The differences are tiny (about 0.03, under 1% of the error) and well within the noise for only 99 test observations, so no model is clearly better. The CV results agree: ridge (4.759) and forward selection (4.757) are essentially tied, both only slightly ahead of the linear model (4.804).

Forward selection kept 11 of 13 covariates, dropping only indus and age. Ridge chose λ ≈ 8.5, which is mild shrinkage: with 13 predictors and 407 training observations, ordinary least squares overfits little, so the penalty has little to fix.

Since accuracy does not separate the models, the choice should rest on interpretability. The forward-selected or full linear model is a reasonable pick, with ridge as an alternative if stability under correlated covariates matters more.
